sheet-1.description: Sheet 1 of the 1924 Hamburg atlas, drawn at 100 ft to an inch, covers the northern and eastern residential part of the borough. Wantage Avenue (today Hamburg Turnpike) runs up the left edge of the sheet from the Church Street and Orchard Street corner at the lower left; from it Vernon Avenue runs north-east across the sheet, crossed by Card Avenue, Oak Street, Lehigh, Lawrence and a street lettered Not Named, with Linwood Avenue parallel to the south and Huron Place joining Lehigh and Lawrence at the bottom. Oak Street leaves Wantage opposite Wallkill Avenue and bends south-east across Vernon and Linwood. Most of the sheet is frame dwellings with stables and outbuildings on deep lots, many shown only as scattered houses on large unsubdivided blocks. Near Wantage Avenue are the Church of Good Shepherd, a fire department house, a garage, the Hamburg Inn, the post office, a printing shop and the Hamburg Gospel Mission; on Card Avenue is the John McKay Gospel Mission, and between Oak and Lehigh the public schools, one brick and one frame. The upper right of the sheet carries the title cartouche, the key, a New Jersey locator map, the index of specials and a key map of the town at 800 ft to an inch; these are left out of the mask, so the mapped area is the left strip along Wantage Avenue and the lower two thirds of the sheet. A bar scale is drawn at the bottom centre.
notes: Wantage (Avenue) is today Hamburg Turnpike (NJ 23).
Oak (Street) east of Wantage is today part of Wallkill Avenue.
Card Avenue is today Card Street; Lawrence is today Lawrence Street; Huron Place lies on today's Hamilton Street.
Lehigh has no clear modern counterpart in OpenStreetMap and was not used for control.
Church Street is today part of Hamburg Turnpike.
Huron Place is lettered 'arbitrary', meaning a name assigned by the mapmaker.

Scale 100 ft. Map of Wantage Av (Hamburg Turnpike), Vernon Av, Oak St (now Wallkill Avenue east of the turnpike), Card Av, Linwood Av, Lehigh St, Lawrence St, Huron Pl; title, key, index, NJ locator and an 800 ft key map in the upper part are cut out of the mask. One part.

sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 of the 1924 Hamburg atlas, drawn at 50 ft to an inch, covers the western business and railroad side of the borough. Wallkill Avenue crosses the sheet from the south-west, where it is drawn at an angle, to Wantage Avenue (today Hamburg Turnpike) at the right edge, opposite the end of Oak Street. Orchard Street runs north-south through the middle of the sheet and turns east at the bottom to meet Wantage, Church Street and Vernon Avenue at the lower right corner; Main Street leaves Orchard at the bottom edge. The New York, Susquehanna and Western Railroad crosses the left half of the sheet, with its station and freight house beside Wallkill Avenue. West of the tracks is the Diamond Dairy Creamery with an ice house and separating building, and a large paper storage building; east of them the Reeve Harden flour, feed and grain business with coal pockets, a lumber shed, an ice house and a concrete flour, feed and grain warehouse, and oil tanks elevated on piles. The Hotel National stands at the corner of Wallkill Avenue and Orchard Street. The rest of the sheet is frame dwellings with stables and garages on narrow lots along Orchard Street and Wantage Avenue, and large open blocks in the upper left. A bar scale is drawn at the bottom and a compass rose at the upper left.
notes: Wantage (Avenue) is today Hamburg Turnpike (NJ 23).
The east-west stretch of Orchard Street at the bottom of the sheet is followed today by Ames Boulevard; the modern Orchard Street leaves the old line south of the bend.
Reeve Harden, Flour, Feed and Grain, and the Diamond Dairy Creamery are listed in the specials index on sheet 1.
Sheet 2 fits about 7 percent larger than its drawn scale against modern junctions (8.4 against about 7.9 px/ft on the other 50 ft sheet).
Scale 50 ft. Wallkill Av, Orchard St, Wantage Av (Hamburg Turnpike), Vernon Av at the lower right; NYS&W station and freight house, Reeve Harden flour and feed, Diamond Dairy Creamery. One part.

sheet-3-1.description: Right-hand part of sheet 3 of the 1924 Hamburg atlas, drawn at 50 ft to an inch: the business centre of the borough around Main Street, separated by a heavy line from the left part of the sheet, which shows South Street further south. Orchard Street crosses the top of the part, with Vernon Avenue entering at the upper right; Main Street runs south from Orchard and then bends south-east to join South Street, and Church Street runs south from Linwood Avenue to become South Street (today Hamburg Turnpike). Along Main Street are brick and frame stores, a bank with a school annex, a drug store, paints and oils, a lodge room, an ice cream works, a vacant store, a blacksmith and a wheelwright; between Main and Church Streets are stores, a tin shop, a bowling alley with an undertaker and hall above, and a concrete storage building. East of Church Street are the First Baptist Church and a cemetery. In the open lower half of the part lies the Ice Pond with an ice house and a milk building beside it, a large garage for ninety cars on South Street, and the New York, Susquehanna and Western Railroad curving down the left side. A match line lettered A and B near the bottom marks where the left part of the sheet continues. A bar scale is drawn at the bottom.
notes: Church (Street) and South (Street) are today Hamburg Turnpike (NJ 23).
Orchard Street at the top of the part is followed today by Ames Boulevard; the modern Orchard Street joins Main Street further south on a new line.
The modern junction of Main Street with Hamburg Turnpike lies about 90 m from where the drawn Main Street meets South Street and was not used.
Control is three junctions near the top of the part; the lower half has none.

Scale 50 ft. Two parts split by a heavy vertical line: part 1 (right) Main St, Church St (Hamburg Turnpike), Orchard St, Linwood Av, South St, Ice Pond; part 2 (left) South St (Hamburg Turnpike) with Stone Mill Rd (Gingerbread Castle Road), L&HRR trestle, Otway Rd (Wishing Well Road) and High St (Oak Street) at the bottom; part 2 continues south of part 1 (match line A-B).

sheet-3-2.description: Left-hand part of sheet 3 of the 1924 Hamburg atlas, drawn at 50 ft to an inch and separated from the business centre on the right by a heavy line. It shows South Street (today Hamburg Turnpike) running down the middle of the part south of the match line lettered A and B at the top, which joins it to the bottom of the right part. Stone Mill Road leaves South Street towards the south-west, and at the bottom Otway Road comes in from the west and High Street goes off to the east, opposite each other at South Street. The Lehigh and Hudson River Railroad crosses the part diagonally from the lower left and passes over South Street on an iron trestle, with a siding and coal pockets beside it in the block between Stone Mill Road and South Street. A curving lane leaves South Street in the lower right. The part is thinly built: a few frame dwellings, a stable, a concrete garage and a concrete storage building, with most of the blocks left open. Block numbers 7, 21 and 22 are lettered on it.
notes: South (Street) is today Hamburg Turnpike (NJ 23).
Stone Mill Road near South Street is today Gingerbread Castle Road; further west it is Wheatsworth Road.
Otway Road is today Wishing Well Road and High (Street) is today Oak Street.
Otway Road is lettered 'arbitrary', a name assigned by the mapmaker.
Placed from two points, one of them hand-picked (South Street and Stone Mill Road); low confidence.

Scale 50 ft. sheet-4-1.description: Main part of sheet 4 of the 1924 Hamburg atlas, drawn at 100 ft to an inch, covering the southern end of the borough between the Wallkill River and South Street (today Hamburg Turnpike). South Street runs down the middle of the sheet from High Street, where the Presbyterian Church stands, to Ripley Place at the bottom. West of it Otway Road runs south from High Street, crossed by Haines Street, and meets Morgan Street, which continues south to Ripley Place; Rarden Place joins Morgan and South Streets, and a diagonal street links Otway Road with South Street. High Street, lined with frame dwellings, runs east along the top. In the upper left Stone Mill Road crosses the Wallkill on an iron bridge beside the Wallkill Roller Flour Mills, with the tail race and a concrete flume. The New York, Susquehanna and Western and the Lehigh and Hudson River railroads run south through the middle left with a freight house. In the lower left, below a dam on the Wallkill, is the large plant of the Union Waxed and Parchment Paper Company, with beater, machine, finishing and shipping rooms, a waxing building, tenements and a description of its fire protection. Steep Hill is lettered west of the river. The residential blocks are frame dwellings on large lots. The right side of the sheet, behind a heavy line, is a separate part.
notes: South (Street) is today Hamburg Turnpike (NJ 23); High (Street) is today Oak Street.
Otway Road is today Wishing Well Road; Haines (Street) is today Governor Haines Street.
Morgan (Street) and the diagonal street to South Street are today King Cole Road; Rarden Place is today Urban Street; Ripley Place is today Prince Street.
Stone Mill Road is today Wheatsworth Road west of the railroads.
Otway Road, Rarden Place and Ripley Place are lettered 'arbitrary', names assigned by the mapmaker.

Scale 100 ft. Two parts: part 1 (main) South St (Hamburg Turnpike) from High St to Ripley Pl, Otway Rd, Haines St, Morgan St, Rarden Pl, Wallkill River, Union Waxed and Parchment Paper Co, Wallkill Roller Flour Mills; part 2 (right inset, behind a heavy line) South St south of Ripley Pl to the borough limit and creek.

sheet-4-2.description: Right-hand part of sheet 4 of the 1924 Hamburg atlas, drawn at 100 ft to an inch and set off from the main part by a heavy line. It continues South Street (today Hamburg Turnpike) south of Ripley Place, which is drawn again at the top with the end of Morgan Street, down to the borough limits and a creek crossed by a concrete bridge at the bottom of the sheet. A siding of the Lehigh and Hudson River Railroad runs along the creek. The part is almost all one large block, number 27, with scattered frame dwellings and outbuildings along the west side of South Street and a group of buildings at the lower right; the rest of the block is open. Its own north arrow is drawn in the middle of the part. The house numbers along South Street run in the 400s, continuing those of the main part.
notes: South (Street) is today Hamburg Turnpike; Ripley Place is today Prince Street; Morgan Street is today King Cole Road.
Ripley Place is lettered 'arbitrary', a name assigned by the mapmaker.
Placed from one hand-picked junction (Morgan Street and Ripley Place) with the scale and rotation of the main part of the sheet; low confidence, especially at the south end.
